reactToFigmaNotes: panel flattens Base UI's data-panel-open trigger attribute into a design-only expanded/collapsed axis; the panel's real height (--accordion-panel-height) is written by a runtime ResizeObserver and has no static value, so it is modelled as a state rather than a size. The panel node is gated `when: { panel: "open" }` so a closed item materializes no panel at all, rather than a panel with visible-but-clipped content.

The open-item background lift reads Base UI's own `data-open` on the item (`[data-ui="accordion-item"][data-open]`). The `panel` axis maps open to `[data-panel-open]`, which the trigger and the panel carry; `partValueSelectors` gives the item part its own `[data-open]`, so the item's fill binds in the open cells.

accordion-trigger-icon rotates 180deg on open ([data-panel-open] [data-ui="accordion-trigger-icon"] { rotate: 180deg }) — neither the resolved plan nor the plugin walker has a rotation field (there is no rotation field anywhere in the pipeline). Faking it with a second static icon asset would misrepresent a CSS transform as a different icon, so the icon is emitted identically (unrotated) in every documented example instead.

`content` is the body of each panel: a panel accepts arbitrary children, so it is a native slot that stretches across the item, and the paragraph from the documented example is only its default content. A designer can replace it with anything. Where a Figma build has no native slots, the same paragraph is placed as an ordinary frame in the same position, so the panel looks identical. The slot sits on the panel, so every item instance carries its own.

reactToFigmaNotes: AlertDialog has no React-facing visual axes: the open/closed transition is a runtime mount concern, not a stylable variant, so this contract documents the single shown state (title + description) — identical reasoning to Dialog, and to popover/tooltip/preview-card.

AlertDialog is CSS-identical to Dialog (same backdrop/popup/title/description rules, alert-dialog.css vs dialog.css) — the two contracts diverge only in slug/part names, mirroring how the components themselves diverge only in Base UI primitive (`AlertDialog` enforces a non-dismissible, confirmation-only modal at the React layer; nothing about that distinction is expressible in CSS or a Figma variant).

`context` is design-only and has no React prop. `context=viewport` (default) generates the popup centred inside a viewport stand-in frame whose width binds the existing `web/breakpoint/view` variable (switch the web mode to see sm/md/lg), whose height hugs the popup plus padding, and whose alert-dialog-backdrop renders from alert-dialog.css. The popup's `min(calc(100vw - var(--spacing-600)), 480px)` width is computed when the contract is built: the popup fills the frame inside `spacing/600` padding on each side (the token the CSS margin names), capped at 480px. `context=component` is the bare popup, as generated before the frame existed. Identical mechanism to Dialog's. The component-set root of the viewport variant is the frame; Code Connect and the documentation page map the popup, not the frame, to <AlertDialog>.

alert-dialog-trigger is a `data-slot` render-target with no `data-ui` and no co-located CSS, rendered OUTSIDE alert-dialog-popup entirely (a sibling in the DOM, not a descendant) — unlike the two AlertDialogClose buttons below, it cannot be modelled as a child of this contract's root without inventing structure that doesn't exist in the real DOM. Left undocumented here rather than faked, the same treatment popover.figma.contract.ts gives popover-trigger.

alert-dialog-header and alert-dialog-footer are the real `AlertDialog.Header` and `AlertDialog.Footer` parts. The header stacks the title over the description; the footer is a row aligned to the end (`gap: var(--spacing-200)`), and both layouts and gaps are derived from alert-dialog.css. The footer stacks in reverse order below the small breakpoint; that rule sits behind a viewport media query, so the generated footer is the row. The two AlertDialogClose buttons in the documented example ("Keep account" — variant="secondary" mode="ghost" — and "Delete" — variant="destructive") are inside alert-dialog-footer, so each is a composedChild Button instance. Each sits in a frame the markup does not author, because a composed child needs a frame to hold the instance.

omittedParts.autocomplete-trigger: Real (`[data-ui="autocomplete-trigger"]`), but not composed by either of Autocomplete's documented examples — its own CSS comment calls it "rare; group is usually the field". reactToFigmaNotes: autocomplete-root is a synthetic, unpainted vertical root (no data-ui source part) holding autocomplete-input-group, the real, styled field surface, and below it autocomplete-popup, gated `when: { popup: ["open", "open-empty"] }`. The field's fill, border and radius bind on the field part. No positioning fields are declared.

popup, state and validity flatten Base UI runtime state into design variants of the field (closed/open/open-with-no-results, default/hover/focus-visible/disabled, valid/invalid). `popup` holds the results too: `open-empty` is the popup with no results (`data-empty`), shown with `autocomplete-empty` instead of `autocomplete-list`. validity maps to the real, reflected Base UI attribute `data-invalid`, which this component's own CSS layer styles on the field. The focus ring is the State value `focus-visible` (the field's `:focus-within` outline), not the `focus-visible` boolean property: the ring layer is generated only from a root `:focus-visible` outline, and this root is synthetic.

The item is the `autocomplete-item` Building Block, whose highlighted and disabled states are its own variants; the popup holds an instance of it. It has no selected state: Autocomplete never selects an item (Base UI fixes its selection mode to none).

autocomplete-clear renders unconditionally (matching the docs example's own unconditional JSX) rather than being gated on Base UI's runtime data-filled attribute, which this component's own CSS layer doesn't style differently anyway.

autocomplete-item-label is a synthetic text child: Autocomplete.Item renders its label directly as text content with no wrapping data-ui element. It inherits its textStyle from autocomplete-item's own CSS (font-family/size/weight/line-height/color declared directly on the item).
No item-check/ItemIndicator part exists — Autocomplete.Item has no such sub-component (unlike Combobox.ItemIndicator).
The trigger/icon disclosure control, backdrop, arrow, row layout primitive, and status live-region are omitted — see `omittedParts` for the specific, individually-reasoned gap each represents.

reactToFigmaNotes: `shape` reflects Avatar's real `data-shape` prop; it's declared as a design-only axis here only because `shape` isn't in the CSS-resolver's auto-derived variant hint list (`VARIANT_PROP_HINTS`) — the same reason Checkbox's `state`/`validity` are also declared this way despite being real DOM attributes.

contract.capReason: A text button's size, content and state are one grid a designer reads across. Splitting a third axis out would make 60 sets of 16, to save two variants over the 30-variant guideline.
reactToFigmaNotes: state is a design-only display axis. `disabled` is the React disabled prop; `hover` and `active` are browser states (`:hover`, `:active`) with no prop to set.

content groups the React icon-only and child-content combinations into stable Figma examples: `icon-label` is `data-has-icon` (a direct child with `data-icon`, or an svg), `icon-only` is `data-icon-only` (any `icon*` size). variant and mode split the output into one set each (`Primary Filled Button`), so a Code Connect template fixes both props and reads size, content and state from the instance.

reactToFigmaNotes: `size` maps 1:1 to the React `size` prop (`data-size`, default `md`). It sets the padding and the gap only, and every part follows it; the title and the content keep the same type at every size.
`footer` is design-only: React has no prop for it, a card simply has or lacks a `Card.Footer` child. `actions` generates the footer with the documented Cancel and Save buttons as its default content.

The surface is an Elevated: the fill, border and shadow bind the page default (surface level 3, shadow level 1). In code a card inside another card lands two surface levels higher with the same shadow level; place a Card inside a Card's content slot in Figma and set its fill to the next surface level by hand.

`content` and `footer` are native slots: the regions accept arbitrary children, and the documented sentence and buttons are only their default content. Where a Figma build has no native slots, the same nodes are placed as ordinary frames.
`card-action` is not generated (see `omittedParts`). The header's title and description stack vertically.

Checked and validity flatten Base UI runtime states into design variants. State is the standard design-only axis: `disabled` is the React disabled prop; `hover` and `focus-visible` are browser states with no prop to set.

CheckboxGroup has no design-facing axes of its own — value/defaultValue/onValueChange/allValues/disabled are runtime coordination concerns, not visual variants; disabled state renders on each composed Checkbox instance (checkbox.figma.contract.ts), not the group.
Each item's default content is a Checkbox instance: editing Checkbox propagates to every CheckboxGroup that composes it.

The docs example wraps each Checkbox in a `Field.Label`. Each row is a synthetic frame with the Checkbox instance and a FieldLabel instance (field-label.figma.contract.ts, built from Field's stylesheet), so the label's text style and colour are Field's. Each row's text is the docs example's, set on the instance (`items[].slots`); the instance stays linked to FieldLabel.

checkbox-group.css has no paint/text CSS of its own — the composed-only-wrapper exception (the compiler's isComposedOnlyWrapper check) allows this contract to compile without an own CSS-derived binding because its only required slot composes an already-contracted component.
